stem.text: Fig. 10.1 is a diagram of part of a neurone membrane while the resting potential is maintained.

stem.caption: Fig. 10.1
stem.alt: Diagram of part of a neurone membrane, drawn as two interlocking channel-protein shapes spanning the membrane between tissue fluid (above) and axoplasm (below), labelled 'cell surface membrane'. Above the membrane in the tissue fluid, two triangles sit above an arrow pointing down into one channel. Below the membrane in the axoplasm, three circles sit near an arrow pointing up into the other channel, and a square sits near a short diagonal arrow pointing up into a small protrusion on that same channel.

stem.text: On Fig. 10.1, use label lines and letters to label:

markScheme.note: This is a labelling task on the figure itself (draw label lines and letters), not a written answer; the two MS marks are for correctly placed K and A labels.

explanation.text: At resting potential the membrane is maintained by the sodium–potassium pump using ATP, and leaky potassium channels. The three circles shown just below the membrane in the axoplasm represent potassium ions (K+) about to be pumped out, so the label K points to those circles or the channel moving them. The square near the small protrusion on the pump structure represents the ATP molecule that powers the pump (its hydrolysis drives the active transport), so A labels that square or the site where it acts. The triangles above the membrane, moving down into the other channel, represent sodium ions (Na+) leaking back in — these are not labelled in this question.

reasoningChain: Identify the sodium-potassium pump structure, which uses ATP to move ions against their gradients.
The three circles moving out represent K+ — label K there.
The square powering the pump represents ATP — label A there.

inferredMistakes.text: Labelling the triangles (which represent Na+ moving in a different channel) as K, confusing the ion shown leaking in through one channel with the ion actively pumped out through the other.

stem.text: Describe the sequence of events that occur during an action potential.

points.text: ref. to threshold (potential) reached (for action potential to occur) ;
AVP ; e.g. entry of sodium ions causes more sodium channels to open

explanation.text: The sequence runs: a stimulus opens some voltage-gated sodium channels, letting Na<sup>+</sup> enter and depolarise the membrane; if this depolarisation reaches the threshold potential, it triggers many more sodium channels to open (positive feedback), causing full depolarisation. Sodium channels then close and voltage-gated potassium channels open, so K<sup>+</sup> leaves the axon, repolarising the membrane. Because potassium channels stay open slightly too long, the membrane potential briefly overshoots below the normal resting value (hyperpolarisation) before the sodium-potassium pump restores the resting potential.

reasoningChain: Stimulus → some Na+ channels open → depolarisation begins.
If threshold is reached, many more Na+ channels open → full depolarisation.
K+ channels open, Na+ channels close → repolarisation.
Slight overshoot (hyperpolarisation) → return to resting potential.

inferredMistakes.text: Describing only depolarisation (sodium entry) without going on to describe repolarisation and the potassium-driven return to resting potential, missing half the sequence the question asks for.

stem.text: Table 10.1 shows the axon diameter, myelination and transmission speed of impulses of motor neurones for three animals: squid, cockroach and cat.
Describe and suggest explanations for the results shown in Table 10.1.

points.text: myelinated axon / myelination, produces faster transmission speed (than unmyelinated) ;
a larger the diameter (for unmyelinated) results in a faster transmission speed ; ora
myelination has a greater effect on transmission speed than axon diameter ;

alternatives: action potential jumps from node (of Ranvier) to node ;

points.text: axons with wider diameter have, less ion leakage / larger surface area / lower resistance ;

markScheme.note: The MS prints two unnumbered sub-headings, "description" and "explanation", above two groups of marking points; stored here as points 1 and 5 with numberedInMs: false so they display as headings rather than numbered marks.

explanation.text: Comparing the three rows: the cat (myelinated, narrowest axon) has by far the fastest transmission (100 m/s), faster than the squid (unmyelinated but widest axon, 30 m/s) and the cockroach (unmyelinated, narrow axon, slowest at 10 m/s). Within the two unmyelinated axons, the wider squid axon is faster than the narrower cockroach axon — a larger diameter normally speeds transmission because it gives a greater surface area and lower resistance to current flow, so less current leaks out per unit length and the impulse travels faster. But the cat's result shows myelination outweighs diameter: despite having a far narrower axon than the squid, the cat transmits over three times faster, because myelination allows saltatory conduction — the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next rather than regenerating continuously along the whole membrane, which is a much faster mechanism than relying on diameter alone.

reasoningChain: Compare the two unmyelinated axons: wider (squid) is faster than narrower (cockroach), consistent with diameter affecting speed.
Compare the myelinated cat to both unmyelinated animals: despite the narrowest diameter, it is fastest.
Conclude myelination (saltatory conduction) has a bigger effect on speed than diameter.
Explain each effect: myelination → saltatory conduction; diameter → less ion leakage / lower resistance.

inferredMistakes.text: Concluding that axon diameter has no effect on speed at all, rather than that myelination simply has the larger effect — the squid/cockroach comparison still shows diameter does matter between two otherwise similar (unmyelinated) axons.
